brief.title: AI copilot pilot adoption among US small businesses
brief.description: A directional hypothesis about pilot governance, workflow fit, and responsible adoption.
brief.researchIntent: Identify the controls that might make a bounded AI-copilot pilot credible to smaller employer businesses.
brief.disclosure: Synthetic, model-generated hypothesis—not observed survey results or a market estimate.
brief.evidenceBoundary: Census data may establish firm-size, sector, and AI-use context; NIST may define risk-management considerations. Neither source establishes product preference, pilot intent, purchase likelihood, workforce impact, or the accuracy of this synthetic distribution.
brief.humanValidation: Conduct 12–15 decision-maker interviews, a message-and-control conjoint with a properly recruited business sample, and an observed 60-day pilot measuring opt-in, weekly use, review burden, error escalation, and discontinuation.

request.prompt: How likely would you be to approve a 60-day AI-copilot trial for drafting and internal knowledge search if every output required human review, business data was contractually protected, and monthly cost was capped?
request.audience: Owners and operations, IT, or functional decision-makers at United States employer businesses with 20–249 employees
request.assumptions: Low-risk internal workflows only; no automated employment decisions; onboarding and opt-out are included; no staffing-reduction promise; contractual data controls work as described.

study.title: Likelihood to approve a 60-day AI-copilot trial for drafting andinternal
study.summary: Synthetic responses suggest cautious openness to a short, tightly governed AI-copilot trial for drafting and internal knowledge search among U.S. employer businesses with 20–249 employees. Support is concentrated in the middle and upper-mid
study.takeaway: The model-generated distribution suggests conditional approval is more likely when the trial is time-limited, human-reviewed, data-protected, and cost-capped; some model cells still indicate a need for proof of accuracy, control, and fit before broader use.

responses.quote: I can see the value, but I would still want a very narrow pilot. If it slips on accuracy even occasionally, the review burden can erase the benefit.

responses.quote: The trial sounds reasonable if permissions are tight and the outputs stay internal. I am not ready to call it a yes until I see how it handles our real documents.

responses.profile: A functional leader responsible for a small team and repetitive writing work
responses.quote: A short trial with mandatory review feels like a practical way to test whether it saves time without exposing us to much downside.

responses.profile: An owner-operator who wants a capped experiment before any broader investment
responses.quote: I would likely approve it because the guardrails make it feel contained. A 60-day test is long enough to learn, but short enough to stop if it does not help.
